example.answer: The monthly payment is $1,896.20, the total paid is $682,633.47, and the total interest is $382,633.47.
example.problem: You borrow $300,000 at 6.5% annual interest over 30 years. What is the monthly payment, and how much interest do you pay in total?
example.title: A 30-year home loan

faqs.a: Use the formula with your numbers, or this calculator. For example, $300,000 at 6.5% over 30 years gives about $1,896.20 per month in principal and interest.
faqs.q: How do I calculate my monthly mortgage payment?

faqs.a: A 15-year term has a higher monthly payment but far less total interest, because the rate is usually lower and you pay for half the time. On the $300,000 example above, a 15-year loan at 6% would cost roughly $2,531.57 per month but only about $155,682 in total interest.

The monthly rate is the annual rate divided by 12. A 6.5% annual rate becomes 0.54167% per month (0.0054167 as a decimal), not simply 6.5 ÷ 12 percent of the balance each time, because each payment also reduces the balance.
faqs.q: Why do I divide the annual rate by 12?

faqs.a: This calculator shows principal and interest only. Your actual monthly bill usually also includes property tax, homeowner's insurance, and possibly private mortgage insurance (PMI), often combined as PITI.
faqs.q: Does this include taxes and insurance?

formula.label: Monthly payment
formula.note: P is the loan amount, r the monthly rate, n the number of payments

formula.label: Total interest
formula.note: What you pay overall minus what you borrowed

howItWorks: A mortgage is paid in equal monthly installments that cover both interest and principal. The calculator first converts your annual rate to a monthly rate and your years to a number of payments, then applies the standard amortization formula: payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n). Each payment chips away at the balance, so early payments are mostly interest and later ones mostly principal.

This is an estimate for planning purposes, not financial advice. Real mortgages also include property tax, insurance, and possibly PMI on top of principal and interest, and actual rates depend on your credit, down payment, and lender. Always confirm figures with a lender or mortgage advisor before borrowing.
intro: Work out the monthly payment on a home loan, plus how much you will pay in total and how much of that is interest. Enter the loan amount, the annual interest rate, and the term in years.

mistakes.text: The formula divides by the monthly rate (annual ÷ 12). Using 6.5 directly instead of 0.0054167 makes the payment impossibly large.
mistakes.title: Forgetting to convert the annual rate to a monthly rate

mistakes.text: Thirty years means 360 payments, not 30. Forgetting the ×12 step understates the total interest dramatically.
mistakes.title: Using years instead of number of payments

mistakes.text: The monthly payment here is principal and interest only. Your real bill adds property tax, insurance, and possibly PMI, which can add hundreds per month.
mistakes.title: Thinking the payment is the whole bill

mistakes.text: Over 30 years at 6.5%, the interest on $300,000 exceeds the loan itself. A shorter term or extra principal payments cut total interest far more than most borrowers expect.
mistakes.title: Underestimating total interest on long terms
